output.headline: Burnham rules out snap election to focus on delivering for voters
output.standfirst: Labour's recovery in the polls had fuelled talk of a snap election, but the prime minister says he will focus on delivering — including reform of the water industry — until 2029
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham has confirmed he will not call a general election before 2029, ruling out days of speculation that Labour's revival in the polls could tempt him into an early contest.

The prime minister addressed the question repeatedly during a round of broadcast interviews with regional media on Friday, setting out his focus on delivering rather than an early poll.

He said he was “not particularly” tempted by the idea at first, then became firmer, saying he would “knock that dead” and was “not going to do that” because he was focused on getting on with the job.

Asked by ITV Calendar whether the next election would be in 2029, Burnham said: “Well, yes, that's when the next election will be. All of this speculation on an early election – I can knock that dead.

“You know, people want me, new in office, to be getting on with the job of delivering on the things that we've discussed, rather than putting self-serving politics before that, which was what I would be doing if I call an election. I'm not going to do that.”

Talk of an early election had grown during the last week after polls showed Labour pulling into the lead with support in the low 20s, with the Conservatives and Reform neck-and-neck a few points behind.

Westminster sources said Downing Street advisers and MPs had been weighing the merits of an early poll, though even with the right split, Labour would risk losing its majority and having to form a coalition.

The Guardian revealed on Friday that Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour's 2024 manifesto, is taking on a senior role advising John Healey, the chancellor, to strengthen his team before the budget — fuelling further speculation that the party's campaign preparations were gathering pace.

Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, devised Keir Starmer's five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour's approach to government.

Healey recruited Athwal as his senior special adviser from the business advisory group Flint Global, previously run by Burnham's chief of staff, James Purnell, a Blair-era cabinet minister.

All parties had stepped up preparations for a potential campaign since Burnham replaced Starmer in the summer, in case he chose to capitalise on the bounce in his popularity.

The prime minister has repeatedly ruled that out, both before and after taking office, telling his regional interviews that his attention was on the party's autumn conference — including setting out more details of a new model for the water industry that increases public control.

He told BBC South: “As we go into the Labour conference, we will set out more thinking about the change that we need to see in the running of water across the country. But it is clear to me that what we've had in the last 30 years is nowhere near good enough and is actually letting the public pay.”

Burnham also confirmed reports that he would not give any exclusive interviews or articles to the Sun, a policy of solidarity with victims of the Hillsborough disaster over the newspaper's coverage of the 1989 tragedy, which falsely blamed Liverpool fans for the deaths of supporters and for which it has since apologised.

Ahead of the conference in Liverpool, Labour members have been cheered by Burnham's takeover, which has led to a modest recovery in the party's popularity.

An MRP poll of more than 8,000 voters, reported by the Guardian this week, showed a significant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham's Labour, encouraging those in the party who had been weighing an early election while Reform's ratings ebb and leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum.

Twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right since April, according to previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, conducted by Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees in Burnham's first month as prime minister.

It also showed progressive voters could push Reform UK into fourth place and put Labour within touching distance of a majority if tactical voting were widespread.

Burnham is beginning to attract a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage, the results suggest.
output.progress: Burnham says his autumn conference speech will set out plans to increase public control of the water industry.
